node.label: Sheila Rowbotham
node.date_label: Women, Resistance and Revolution (1972) · Hidden from History (1973) · Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973) · Beyond the Fragments (1979) · A Century of Women (1997)
node.description: Hidden from History (1973) argues that women’s work and collective resistance belong at the centre of social history, with class differences preventing any simple story of universal sisterhood or steady progress. Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973) connects feminist consciousness to changing material life, while asking how domestic labour, childrearing and inner experience exceed existing Marxist explanations. Gillian Scott’s 1998 review of A Century of Women valued its integration of women into wider social transformation. Intellectual debts also brought disagreement: Rowbotham recalled E. P. Thompson criticizing the assumption that experiencing oppression necessarily gives someone the best understanding of it. She accepted the need for qualifications, while rejecting the Thompsons’ suspicion that the movement was imposing ideas drawn from its members’ limited experience as young middle-class women. Her later work combines historical recovery with criticism of fixed accounts of gender domination.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Women, Resistance and Revolution (1972); Hidden from History (1973); Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973); Socialism and the New Life (1977), with Jeffrey Weeks; Beyond the Fragments (1979), with Lynne Segal and Hilary Wainwright; A Century of Women (1997); Threads Through Time (1999); Promise of a Dream (2000).
node.scope_note: Selected author retrospectives, interview passages, a translated lecture, contemporary reviews and bibliographic records read. Selected books and the original 1979 patriarchy essay remain unread. The Thompsons’ criticism is reported through Rowbotham’s recollection; the English 2012 lecture and Alexander–Taylor response were not read. Restricted interview bodies were not accessed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rowbotham recalls that Thompson's The Making of the English Working Class (1963), which she read in proof, made “a profound impression” on her through its account of how economic transformation affected daily experience and gave rise to an emergent consciousness among people without power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: LEHMT, English paragraphs beginning “He was in the process” and “His account”; “made a profound impression upon me”. Her retrospective testimony is read; Thompson’s complete book is unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Remembering Dorothy and Edward (2012), Rowbotham credits Dorothy Thompson’s respect for local activists and insistence on examining original evidence as formative historical examples.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Spanish translation, p. 142: “activistas locales”, “datos originales”; her 1964 adult-education research is explicitly recalled. Self-reported influence; Dorothy’s cited books and English lecture unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Dorothy Thompson: evidence and ordinary activists

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2025 Nueva Sociedad interview, Rowbotham identifies Hobsbawm as supervisor of the doctorate she began in 1964 on the University Extension movement.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Supervision question and answer: “Mi supervisor de tesis fue Eric Hobsbawm”. She expressly distinguishes admiration from political influence. The 2014 retrospective records abandonment; no completed doctorate asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: Looking back in 2015 on Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973), Rowbotham recalls working within Marx and Engels’ framework while finding Marxist texts “apt to wear somewhat thin” for tracing inner perceptions and material life, or women’s activities in the household and child rearing.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2015 retrospective, paragraphs beginning “If participating” and “But when”; “wear somewhat thin”. Marx and Engels receive joint credit. This retrospective supports qualified criticism, not rejection; original book unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Marx: a resource with feminist limits

proposed_edges.relationship: As recalled in Remembering Dorothy and Edward (2012), Thompson challenged the early women’s liberation claim, initially shared by Rowbotham, that experiencing oppression confers superior authority to write about it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Spanish translation p. 152: “Edward criticó”; Rowbotham accepts a qualified warning about identity-based authority. Retrospectively reported criticism of her movement’s early position, not a review of a named Rowbotham book; English lecture unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reflecting in 2014 on Women, Resistance and Revolution (1972), Rowbotham describes rewriting history with women in mind as a collective endeavour and traces themes from that book into Hidden from History (1973).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Rowbotham’s retrospective on the publisher’s site (18 February 2014), paragraphs beginning Indeed it was eerily evident, I carried on writing, and I could see how rewriting history. These establish the thematic continuity with Hidden from History (1973), the original 1972 publication of Women, Resistance and Revolution, and the collective character of rewriting history with women in mind. This retrospective supports the revised contribution claim; it does not independently establish every claim in the original relationship about exceptional heroines or continuous progress. Selected books remain unread. The separate labour-history edge sr_w_08 retains its existing, explicitly mediated review evidence.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Trouble with Patriarchy (1979) questioned whether an unchanging account of male domination could explain historical variation, women’s agency or cooperation between women and men.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2025 interview, question naming the 1979 essay and following answers: “rigidez ahistórica”. Retrospective account; original essay unread. The interview identifies Alexander and Taylor’s replies without supplying their full arguments.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hidden from History (1973) made women’s overlooked labour and differences between working-class and privileged women part of the history of capitalism and resistance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Kirkus review, paragraphs on production and “hidden labour”. Selected reading supports this labour-history contribution, not a claim that Rowbotham originated all study of women’s work; book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: At History Workshop 4, Rowbotham argued that women's history should be researched as a specific area of study; after the laughter that greeted this, she was among the women who convened Britain's first Women's Liberation Conference at Ruskin (1970), an episode she recounts in Daring to Hope (2021).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Whitehead, “In turn” and “That mocking hostility” paragraphs, explicitly names the memoir. Mediated account; memoir unread. Direct person-to-movement projection complements existing group edge_375; no claim of sole organization or founding.

proposed_edges.relationship: In White, Male and Middle Class (1992), Catherine Hall draws on Sheila Rowbotham’s Hidden from History (1973) to explain early feminist history’s recovery of women’s labour and reproduction.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed chapter preview. Hall identifies Rowbotham’s book as crucial and quotes its question about production and reproduction while discussing the recovery agenda and her own early housewife research. This supports use of a framework, not supervision or a claim that Hall adopted every argument. The complete books were not read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hall: recovering women’s labour and reproduction

proposed_edges.relationship: Julianne Nyhan, Andrew Flinn and Anne Welsh’s ‘Oral History and the Hidden Histories project’ (first published online in 2013) connects the recovery agenda of oral history to the historical exclusion named in Rowbotham’s Hidden from History (1973).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s open text, including the surrounding discussion of recovery, feminist approaches and methodological change. The attribution occurs in the body, not merely the references. Limit this edge to the recovery formulation: it does not establish that Rowbotham invented oral history or its interviewing methods, or a personal debt by a particular timeline oral historian.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hidden from History: oral history’s recovery agenda

proposed_edges.relationship: Barbara Taylor’s 2024 appraisal identifies Rowbotham’s Edward Carpenter: A Life of Liberty and Love (2008) as a major contribution to the pursuit of freely chosen sexuality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Taylor’s complete signed appraisal. The parenthesis explicitly links the biography to sexual freedom. Mapping that historical contribution to the existing Sexuality & queer history field is an editorial classification; Taylor does not name a school or assert an influence on a particular scholar. The biography itself was not read. This is a field edge, not a Taylor-to-Rowbotham review edge.
proposed_edges.map_label: Edward Carpenter: history and sexual freedom
